passage:
Dear Amma and Papa,

I am writing this because at dinner on Sunday I raised my voice, and I don't want that to be the last thing you remember about this. When you said the student climate group is a hobby for people with no future, I felt invisible, like the person you raised had shrunk to a marksheet.

So here are my reasons, calmly. I joined because the lake behind our hostel is dying, and Anjali and I test the water every Saturday morning. I still attend every lecture. My internship form is submitted, and my semester fees are paid from the tutoring money I told you about.

You may still think I am wasting my time. That is allowed. I will keep calling on Thursdays, and I will keep coming home for Diwali.

With love,
Tarun

qa.q: On which day do Tarun and Anjali test the lake water?
qa.a: Tarun and Anjali test the water every Saturday morning.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling at the Sunday dinner, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Tarun felt invisible and hurt, as if the parents saw only a marksheet; the raised voice at dinner shows how much it stung.

qa.q: What makes this letter a wise way to answer the parents?
qa.a: It explains the reasons without blame, points to lectures, the internship form and self-paid fees as proof of responsibility, and accepts that they may still disagree.

qa.q: How might Amma and Papa read this letter?
qa.a: They may still worry about the future, but they can see Tarun is not abandoning studies or family, which may ease their fear even if they keep their view.

grounding: The letter shows a young adult answering parents who dismiss activism by calmly giving reasons, showing responsibility elsewhere and keeping the bond despite disagreement.

So you want the honest version, Madhuri? Fine. I'm Arnab, second-year law, and last winter I started volunteering at the weekend legal help desk for street vendors being evicted near the station. My mother found the photo from the rally on a cousin's phone. She called me that night and said, "You will never get a placement if your face is on a protest banner." My father just said, "Waste." One word. I sat on the hostel stairs for an hour feeling like a stranger in my own family.

What I did next surprised me. I didn't argue that night. On Saturday I went home, showed them my grades, and told them about Shyam uncle, the vendor whose cart we saved. My mother still frowns. But she asked last week if the desk needs old files.

qa.q: Where does Arnab volunteer on weekends?
qa.a: Arnab volunteers at the weekend legal help desk for street vendors being evicted near the station.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel after the phone call with the parents, and what shows it?
qa.a: Arnab felt rejected and alone, like a stranger in the family; sitting on the hostel stairs for an hour shows how deeply it hurt.

qa.q: Why was waiting until Saturday a good choice?
qa.a: Arnab let the heat pass, then explained in person with grades and a real story, so the parents could listen instead of fight.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother see the protest photo differently by the end?
qa.a: She still worries, but asking whether the desk needs old files suggests she is starting to see it as meaningful work, not a threat to Arnab's future.

The municipal reply came on a Tuesday, the same one as always: "Your request is under consideration." Eight months of signatures, two meetings, one sunburnt march to the ward office, and the road outside the college still had no zebra crossing.

Lalit read it standing in the bus shelter while rain hammered the tin roof and his phone battery blinked red. In the group chat Charu had already posted a fresh poster. He typed, "Wow, another poster, that'll fix everything," then stared at it and deleted it.

That night he slept ten hours. On Thursday he told Charu he couldn't carry the whole campaign anymore, but he could do one thing: get the college principal to request a traffic warden at closing time. Charu grinned. "One thing is plenty. Mira aunty from the residents' group has been doing this for years. Come meet her."

qa.q: What did the municipal reply say?
qa.a: It said, "Your request is under consideration."

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he typed the message about the poster?
qa.a: Lalit felt bitter and worn out after eight months with nothing changing, so the sarcasm came from exhaustion and disappointment, not real contempt for Charu.

qa.q: Which of Lalit's choices helped him most, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the mocking message, resting, and choosing one realistic goal, the traffic warden, let him keep going without burning out or hurting Charu.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt if Lalit had sent the sarcastic message?
qa.a: Charu would likely have felt mocked and discouraged for still caring, and the friendship and campaign could both have suffered.

Jahnavi's colony notice board still had her lake poster from March, curling at the corners. Six months of Sunday clean-ups, a petition with nine hundred names, and the drain from the new mall still ran grey into the water.

On Sunday Sonali arrived with a new banner, bright green letters: SAVE OUR LAKE. Jahnavi heard herself say, "Wow, green letters. The builders must be terrified."

Sonali's smile dropped. She rolled the banner up without a word.

Jahnavi felt the words sit in her stomach like a stone. That evening she called. "I'm sorry. I'm just so tired, and I took it out on you." Sonali was quiet, then said, "Me too. Tired, I mean. Want to stop doing everything and just chase the drain complaint?"

They took a week off. Then they went together to the pollution board office with photos of the pipe.

qa.a: The petition had nine hundred names.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling after Sonali rolled up the banner?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty and heavy, the words sitting in her stomach like a stone, because she had mocked someone who still cared.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi and Sonali keep going?
qa.a: An honest apology, a week of rest, and choosing one realistic goal, the drain complaint, instead of trying to do everything.

qa.q: How did Sonali experience Jahnavi's joke about the banner?
qa.a: Sonali felt hurt and mocked for still trying, which is why her smile dropped and she rolled the banner up silently.

grounding: The passage shows a tired campaigner who mocks a friend's effort, then apologises, rests and picks one realistic goal with someone who keeps going.

Subject: about the curfew debate

Ramesh,

You asked why I've gone quiet in the hostel group. Honestly, I'm a bit ashamed. For three weeks I made memes of the pro-curfew students as sheep with lab coats, and I loved the laughing replies. It felt like winning.

Then at the open meeting a first-year girl from their side spoke. Her voice shook. She said she walks back from the library past the unlit construction site and counts her steps. Nobody was calling her a sheep in that room.

I still think a 9 pm curfew is the wrong answer. But I want to argue for lights on that path and a late shuttle, not against her as a person. Can we write a proposal together instead of another meme?

Bhupen

Okay, Irawati, since you're recording, I'll say it straight. My name's Pankaj, I'm twenty, and last year I was the loudest voice against the new highway bypass near our town. I called everyone who supported it idiots. In meetings I'd laugh when they spoke.

Then one evening my scooter broke down and the only open repair shop belonged to Mr Rawat, who'd signed their petition. He fixed it for free and talked while he worked. His son had died in a truck accident on the old road through the market. He wasn't stupid. He was grieving and scared.

I still oppose the route. It cuts through farmland. But now when I speak, I start by saying the old road is dangerous, because it is. People actually listen to me now, including his side.

qa.a: Pankaj now admits the real danger of the old road before arguing against the route, so the other side feels heard and listens back.

qa.a: Mr Rawat may see Pankaj as an opponent who still disagrees but respects his loss, which makes real discussion possible.

The housing collective met every Thursday in a Lisbon café basement, and every Thursday Rui, the founder, found a new reason for another contribution: banners, a lawyer's fee, a van. Gabriel had already given two months of his bakery tips.

This time Gabriel raised his hand. "Could we see where the last collection went? Just a simple list."

The room went quiet. Rui smiled without warmth. "People who ask for receipts are working for the landlords. Are you with us or not?"

On the tram home Yuki said, "You asked what half of us were thinking." Gabriel's hands were still trembling. He felt foolish and angry at once.

The next week he and Yuki visited a tenants' union across the river. Their treasurer pinned the accounts to the noticeboard every month.

qa.q: Where did the housing collective meet every Thursday?
qa.a: It met every Thursday in a Lisbon café basement.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling on the tram home?
qa.a: Gabriel felt foolish and angry at once, and his trembling hands show how shaken he was by being called disloyal.

qa.q: What was wise about Gabriel's question, and what did he do next?
qa.a: Asking for a simple list of how money was used is fair in any real movement; he then found a group that shares its accounts openly.

qa.q: How does Yuki see the moment Gabriel spoke up?
qa.a: Yuki sees it as brave, because many members shared the same doubt but were afraid to be called traitors.

grounding: The scene shows a movement leader answering a request for transparency with accusations of betrayal, and the member treating that as a warning sign.

It was a joke I posted at nineteen, about how my cousin's wedding band played the same song eleven times. Three years later someone cropped out the context and it spread as if I had mocked the whole community. By Saturday night I had four hundred messages. Some called me names I won't repeat. One said they knew my college.

I'm Sonali, and I'll admit the first night I didn't sleep. I kept refreshing, my stomach tight, typing angry replies and deleting them.

On Sunday Ayesha came over with chai. She helped me mute the words, screenshot the threat, and report it to the platform and the college grievance cell before lunch. My hands stopped shaking around evening. I haven't replied to anyone. That was the hardest and best choice.

Hostel counsellor's note, Wednesday.

Lalit came to my office at 11 pm, sent by his roommate Kunal, who had noticed he had not eaten since morning. A short clip of Lalit arguing with a shopkeeper last year had resurfaced, edited to look like he was shouting at an old man for no reason. Strangers were posting his hostel name.

He held his phone with both hands and kept refreshing. He said, "I feel naked. Everyone can see me."

We put the phone face down first. Then, together, we turned off comments, muted his name, and saved screenshots of two messages that mentioned the hostel address. I called the warden that night, and security was told to watch the gate. Lalit phoned his elder sister before sleeping.

Follow-up tomorrow with the college grievance cell. - Maria Fernandes, counsellor

qa.q: What did strangers post about Lalit?
qa.a: Strangers were posting his hostel name.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he said "I feel naked"?
qa.a: Lalit felt exposed and frightened, as if everyone was watching him, which is why he kept refreshing with both hands on the phone.

qa.q: Why was calling the warden that same night important?
qa.a: Two messages mentioned the hostel address, so telling the warden and security the same night made Lalit safer instead of leaving the threat until morning.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt seeing Lalit skip meals all day?
qa.a: Kunal was probably worried and unsure how to help, which is why he sent Lalit to the counsellor.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a student abused by an online crowd being helped to stop refreshing, save evidence, report threats and contact family.

The local bus from Rajgarh to the district college was always late, so Aditi scrolled. Today the town page was on fire. Vinita ma'am, the young tuition teacher from the next lane, had posted that girls should "dress sensibly" for the fair, and hundreds were tearing into her.

Aditi typed, "Maybe dress your brain sensibly first," and watched the laughing reactions climb. Her chest felt warm and buzzing, part of something.

At the fair that evening she passed the tuition centre. Vinita ma'am was sitting on the step, eyes swollen, while her mother spoke sharply to someone on the phone about calls from strangers.

Aditi went home and read the comments again, slowly. Some were fair. Most were just hungry. She deleted hers, then wrote a message to Vinita ma'am saying she disagreed, and why, without the insult.

Exam week, and the hostel Wi-Fi died every evening, so Omkar rationed his data for one thing: the videos of a creator who called himself the Straight Talker. The man said exactly what Omkar felt about unfair entrance exams, and when he tore apart some official, Omkar's heart raced. He shared every clip.

On Thursday his roommate Tenzin, studying under a torch during the power cut, said, "Watch his last three. Count how many times he says 'buy the course'." Omkar laughed it off, then counted anyway. Seven. After each attack came a link to a paid crash course.

Omkar stared at the dim screen. The ideas about exam fairness still made sense. But the anger felt different now, like something being sold to him. He unfollowed, saved two videos he genuinely found useful, and went back to his notes.

qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling after he counted the links?
qa.a: Omkar felt uneasy and a little used, sensing that the anger he enjoyed was being sold to him.

qa.q: What balanced choice did Omkar make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Omkar kept the two useful videos but unfollowed, holding on to good ideas while stepping away from someone profiting from outrage.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the creator compared with Omkar at the start?
qa.a: Tenzin sees a seller using anger to push a course, while Omkar at first saw a hero voicing his own frustration.

grounding: The story shows a young man thrilled by a loud creator who notices the creator profits from outrage and questions him while keeping useful ideas.
